Since only increases in saving are feasible at s₁=0, this sign is consistent with that boundary; it is not proof that the full allocation is optimal. Current leisure has derivative u_l₁−w₁u_c₁=0.24−2(0.12)=0. Future leisure has derivative β(u_l₂−w₂u_c₂)=0.8(0.30−4×0.10)=−0.08. Reducing l₂ by a small δ and consuming the additional 4δ future earnings leaves s₁=0, respects both budgets and gives a strictly positive first-order lifetime utility gain of 0.08δ. The hypothetical borrowing improvement is infeasible.
st.source: Tutorial 5 QP, PDF p1; Tutorial 5 ANS, PDF pp4–19; original borrowing-limit diagnostic
st.rationale: Requires applying a one-sided saving condition, rejecting a tempting but infeasible borrowing improvement, checking both interior leisure conditions and constructing a budget-feasible strict first-order gain.

st.prompt: A worker has U=ln c₁+ln l₁+β(ln c₂+ln l₂), β=0.8, h=10, R=1.25 and w₁=2. Compare unrestricted borrowing with a binding rule s₁≥0 and no initial assets. Future wage rises from 4 to 8. What happens to current labor in the two cases?

choices.text: No borrowing preserves the unrestricted Euler equality at both wages.
choices.feedback: At c₁=10 and future c₂=20 or 40, the desire to borrow is positive; Euler is an inequality at the binding saving constraint.

choices.text: Unrestricted: it falls from 25/9 to zero. No borrowing: it stays at 5.
choices.feedback: Unrestricted workers can finance current leisure using future earnings and reach a time corner. With no borrowing, each current budget finances c₁ from current labor and log utility selects five hours.

choices.text: Both cases reduce current labor to zero.
choices.feedback: Without assets or borrowing, zero current work would force zero current consumption and log utility of negative infinity.

choices.text: Both cases keep current labor at 5.
choices.feedback: Five hours is the separate-date constrained solution, not the unrestricted baseline.

choices.text: Unrestricted: it falls from 25/9 to −5/3. No borrowing: it stays at 5.
choices.feedback: Negative labor is an infeasible continuation of the unrestricted interior formula.

choices.text: Unrestricted: it rises; no borrowing: it falls.
choices.feedback: The future wage raises lifetime wealth and makes future work relatively attractive. These forces do not imply more current unrestricted work.

st.explanation: At w₂=4 the unrestricted interior solution gives n₁=25/9. At w₂=8 its interior l₁ would exceed h; the solution has n₁=0, c₁=c₂=320/13 and l₂=40/13. Under s₁≥0, the optimum remains s₁=0, l₁=l₂=5, c₁=10, while c₂ rises from 20 to 40. The constraint blocks intertemporal financing of current leisure.
st.source: Tutorial 5 QP, PDF p1; Tutorial 5 ANS, PDF pp4–19; borrowing-limit extension within the two-period model
st.rationale: Requires solving and contrasting two constraint regimes, including a time corner and an Euler inequality.

st.prompt: With U=ln c₁+ln l₁+β(ln c₂+ln l₂), β=0.8, h=10, w₁=1 and w₂=4, a worker has no initial assets and may borrow freely. R rises from 1.25 to 2. The initial solution has no current work. Which new allocation and mechanism are valid?

choices.feedback: After the change βR=1.6, so c₂=40/3 rather than c₁.

choices.text: n₁ falls below zero because lifetime wealth falls.
choices.feedback: Leisure cannot exceed h. Moreover, the relative price channel now favors more current work.

choices.text: n₁=5/3, c₁=25/3 and s₁=−20/3; higher R makes current work relatively more valuable and releases the no-work corner.
choices.feedback: The new full income is 30. The interior solution is feasible and has positive current labor despite continued borrowing.

choices.text: n₁=0, c₁=160/13 and s₁=−160/13; the time corner persists at every R.
choices.feedback: The boundary condition changes with R. At R=2, the unconstrained l₁=25/3 is below ten.
Current earnings are 5/3, below consumption 25/3, so saving is negative.

choices.text: n₁=5, c₁=5 and s₁=0 because higher rates prohibit borrowing.
choices.feedback: Borrowing remains permitted; the question changes its price, not its availability.

st.explanation: Full income is 10+40/2=30. Thus c₁=30/3.6=25/3, c₂=0.8×2×25/3=40/3, l₁=25/3 and l₂=10/3. All time bounds are respected. Current income is 5/3 and saving is −20/3. The no-current-work condition is w₂≥Rw₁(1+2β); it holds at 1.25 but fails at 2.
st.source: Tutorial 5 QP, PDF p1; Tutorial 5 ANS, PDF pp4–19; original rate-and-boundary synthesis
st.rationale: Tracks an interest change through wealth, relative wages, a regime switch and saving, rather than applying a single interest arrow.

st.prompt: A zero-asset worker with U=ln c₁+ln l₁+β(ln c₂+ln l₂), h=10 and β=0.8 has an interior allocation with zero saving, w₁=w₂=2 and unrestricted borrowing. After identifying the initial R from optimality, raise R to 2 while wages stay fixed. Which result is correct?

choices.text: Initial R=1.25; new n₁=25/6, n₂=20/3 and s₁=−10/3.
choices.feedback: This reports leisure as labor and reverses the saving sign.

choices.text: Initial R=0.8; new c₂/c₁=0.4.
choices.feedback: The gross return enters Euler multiplicatively: c₂/c₁=βR, not β/R.

choices.text: No initial interior solution can have zero saving.
choices.feedback: At R=1.25, c₁=c₂=10 and l₁=l₂=5 satisfy both budgets and every FOC.

choices.text: Initial R=1.25; new n₁=35/6, n₂=10/3 and s₁=10/3.
choices.feedback: Zero saving first pins down the within-date log allocations; Euler then identifies R. Reoptimization at R=2 produces positive saving.

choices.text: Initial R=1; new saving remains zero.
choices.feedback: Equal wages do not imply R=1 when β<1. Optimal zero saving requires βR=1 here.

choices.text: Initial R=1.25; new n₁=n₂=5 and s₁=0.
choices.feedback: Those are the old separate-date allocations and violate the new Euler condition.

st.explanation: Zero saving implies c_t=w_t(10−l_t). The log leisure condition c_t=w_t l_t gives l_t=5 and c_t=10. Euler gives 1=βR, so R=1.25. At R=2, full income is 30: c₁=25/3, c₂=40/3, l₁=25/6 and l₂=20/3. Therefore n₁=35/6, n₂=10/3 and saving 2(35/6)−25/3=10/3.
st.source: Tutorial 5 QP, PDF p1; Tutorial 5 ANS, PDF pp4–19; original inverse and forward application
st.rationale: Combines inverse identification from a zero-saving allocation with forward reoptimization and flow accounting.

st.prompt: For U=ln c₁+ln l₁+β(ln c₂+ln l₂) with β=0.8, h=10 and no assets, wages and the gross return change jointly from (w₁,w₂,R)=(2,4,1.25) to (3,6,1.5). Borrowing is unrestricted and both allocations are interior. Which comparison is correct?

choices.text: Current labor rises and saving becomes positive.
choices.feedback: More work need not imply positive saving. New earnings 95/9 remain below consumption 175/9.

choices.text: Current labor falls because lifetime full income rises.
choices.feedback: The income effect alone cannot determine the net joint change. The full solution gives a labor increase.

choices.text: Saving rises 50% because both wages rise 50%.
choices.feedback: The return also changes; this is not a uniform rescaling of all dated prices and resources.

choices.text: Current consumption stays 130/9 because β is unchanged.
choices.feedback: Full income changes from 52 to 70, so current consumption rises to 175/9.

choices.text: Current labor rises from 25/9 to 95/27, while saving remains −80/9.
choices.feedback: Relative wages alone are unchanged, but R raises the intertemporal reward to current work. Earnings and consumption both rise by five.

choices.text: Current labor is unchanged because both wages rise 50%.
choices.feedback: This ignores the simultaneous change in R and hence in Rw₁/w₂.

st.explanation: Initially c₁=130/9 and n₁=25/9, giving s₁=−80/9. New full income is 30+60/1.5=70, so c₁=175/9, l₁=175/27 and n₁=95/27. New earnings are 95/9 and saving is again −80/9. The unchanged saving is an accounting result of this calibration, not a general invariance theorem.
st.source: Tutorial 5 QP, PDF p1; Tutorial 5 ANS, PDF pp4–19; original simultaneous-shock application
st.rationale: Requires distinguishing wage scaling from a change in the intertemporal price and checking labor, consumption and saving jointly.

st.prompt: An unconstrained representative household has fixed pretax incomes, U=ln c₁+0.8ln c₂ and R=1.2. Government purchases change by ΔG₁=30 and ΔG₂=−36. Simultaneously, current lump-sum taxes fall 20 and future taxes rise 24. Government and household budgets initially balance in present value. What are (ΔC₁, ΔS_private, ΔS_public, ΔS_national)?

choices.feedback: This omits the extra current purchases from public saving.
It treats the tax cut as additional lifetime wealth despite the offsetting future tax.
It treats all extra current purchases as an uncompensated lifetime resource loss.
The tax cut raises private saving when consumption is unchanged and reduces public saving.
National saving is their sum, −30, not +30.
Both tax and purchase changes have zero present value, but current public saving loses 20 of taxes and spends 30 more.

st.explanation: ΔPVG=30−36/1.2=0 and ΔPVT=−20+24/1.2=0. Relative prices and lifetime disposable wealth are unchanged, so consumption is unchanged. Private saving changes by −ΔT₁−ΔC₁=20; public saving by ΔT₁−ΔG₁=−50. National saving changes by −ΔC₁−ΔG₁=−30. Ricardian tax timing does not make a changed current purchase allocation disappear.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 2, PDF pp10–22; original synthesis
st.rationale: Separates two simultaneous present-value-neutral paths from the distinct current private, public and national flows.

st.prompt: At R=1, a household with U=ln c₁+ln c₂, zero assets and incomes after tax (80,160) cannot borrow. Government shifts taxes by cutting current taxes q and raising future taxes q, leaving purchases fixed. What is the smallest q that releases the borrowing constraint, and what are ΔC₁ and ΔS_national when q=60?

choices.text: Threshold q=40; at q=60, ΔC₁=40 and ΔS_national=−40.
choices.feedback: Lifetime resources remain 240, so the unconstrained target remains 120. The cap reaches 120 at q=40; further relief is saved.

choices.text: Threshold q=60; ΔC₁=60 and ΔS_national=−60.
choices.feedback: The consumption ceiling stops binding once current resources reach 120, not 140.

choices.text: Threshold q=40; ΔC₁=0 and ΔS_national=0.
choices.feedback: Neutrality holds only after the constraint is slack; moving from the initially constrained position changes consumption.

choices.text: Threshold q=80; ΔC₁=60 and ΔS_national=−60.
choices.feedback: Equalizing after-tax incomes is sufficient at q=40, and the target remains 120.

choices.text: Threshold q=40; ΔC₁=40 and ΔS_national=+20.
choices.feedback: The +20 is the household saving change. Public saving falls 60, so national saving falls 40.

choices.text: No finite q releases the constraint because lifetime wealth is unchanged.
choices.feedback: The constraint limits current resources, which do change even with unchanged lifetime wealth.

st.explanation: c₁(q)=min(80+q,120) for the stated range. Initially c₁=80 and s₁=0. At q=60 incomes are (140,100), c₁=c₂=120 and s₁=20. Public saving falls 60, so national saving falls 40. At q=40 the constraint is just binding with zero multiplier; it is strictly slack for q>40.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 2, PDF pp10–22; original synthesis
st.rationale: Derives a piecewise policy response across a financing constraint and reconciles household with national saving.

st.prompt: At R=1, household A has U=ln c₁+ln c₂, after-tax incomes (50,150), no assets and no borrowing. A receives a current tax cut of 140, funded by a future tax increase of 140 on unrelated, unconstrained B. Over the entire wealth change, B’s current consumption is a linear function of present-value wealth with constant slope 0.25. B has enough resources to remain unconstrained with positive consumption at both dates. Purchases and pretax incomes stay fixed. What are aggregate ΔC₁ and ΔS_national?

choices.text: ΔC₁=85 and ΔS_national=+55.
choices.feedback: The +55 is aggregate private saving: tax relief of 140 minus consumption growth of 85. Public saving falls 140.

choices.text: ΔC₁=85 and ΔS_national=−85.
choices.feedback: A crosses its borrowing boundary: consumption rises from 50 to 170, a gain of 120. B cuts current consumption by 35.

choices.text: ΔC₁=0 and ΔS_national=0.
choices.feedback: An unchanged aggregate tax PV does not preserve each household budget or erase the constraint.

choices.text: ΔC₁=105 and ΔS_national=−105.
choices.feedback: This assumes A consumes all 140, but after the shift it saves 20.

choices.text: ΔC₁=35 and ΔS_national=−35.
choices.feedback: This applies a one-half wealth MPC to A while ignoring its initially binding constraint.

choices.text: ΔC₁=120 and ΔS_national=−120.
choices.feedback: This omits B’s response to the future tax burden.

st.explanation: A initially wants 100 but can consume only 50. After relief, its incomes are (190,150), so it chooses (170,170) and saves 20. B loses 140 of PV wealth and cuts c₁ by 35. Aggregate consumption rises 120−35=85. At unchanged Y₁ and G₁, national saving falls 85; private saving rises 55 and public saving falls 140.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 2, PDF pp10–22; original synthesis
st.rationale: Combines redistribution, differing consumption responses and a constraint that changes status, rather than assigning fixed MPCs to everyone.

st.prompt: A parent planned a nonnegative bequest of 50 payable next period. R=1.1. Government raises the parent’s current tax by 60 and cuts the child’s future tax by 66. To preserve both generations’ original consumption, only the planned bequest can adjust; negative bequests and reverse transfers are prohibited. Which diagnosis is correct?

choices.text: The parent’s PV shortfall is 16.
choices.feedback: Sixteen is the unoffset future-value shortfall; divide by 1.1 for period-1 units.

choices.text: A bequest of 116 achieves neutrality.
choices.feedback: Increasing transfers worsens the parent’s current resource shortage and adds to the child’s windfall.

choices.text: Neutrality would require a bequest of −16; the zero bound leaves the parent with a PV shortfall of 160/11.
choices.feedback: The parent must reduce future transfers by 66 to offset 60 today. Only 50 can be removed.

choices.text: A bequest of zero achieves complete neutrality.
choices.feedback: Removing 50 future units recovers only 50/1.1 of current resources, less than 60.

choices.text: A bequest of −10 achieves neutrality.
choices.feedback: The tax increase must be carried forward at R, so the required reduction is 66, not 60.

choices.text: The total family tax present value rises by 6.
choices.feedback: The future tax relief of 66 has present value 60, exactly offsetting the current increase.

st.explanation: To recover 60 at date 1, reduce the date-2 bequest by 1.1×60=66. Starting from 50 would require −16, which is infeasible. At zero bequests, the parent recovers 50/1.1 and remains short 60−50/1.1=160/11. Aggregate family PV taxes are unchanged, but the permitted transfer cannot preserve the original allocation.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 2, PDF pp10–22; original synthesis
st.rationale: Checks the feasibility of the offsetting intergenerational transfer and distinguishes future from present shortfalls.

st.prompt: At fixed income and R=1.25, a household’s current consumption response is ΔC₁=−0.4(ΔG₁+ΔG₂/R). Current government purchases rise 60. Choose a future purchase increase that leaves current national saving unchanged. If current taxes rise only 20 and future taxes balance the government budget, which complete package works?

choices.text: ΔG₂=150, ΔT₂=200; national saving is unchanged.
choices.feedback: The purchase PV increase is 180 and C₁ falls 72, so national saving rises 12.

choices.text: ΔG₂=−112.5, ΔT₂=−62.5; private saving rises 40.
choices.feedback: A future purchase cut offsets wealth losses and cannot produce the needed 60 fall in current consumption.

choices.text: ΔG₂=112.5, ΔT₂=162.5; private saving falls 40 and public saving rises 40.
choices.feedback: Current disposable income falls 20 but consumption falls 60, so private saving rises; public saving loses 40.

choices.text: ΔG₂=112.5, ΔT₂=162.5; private saving rises 40 and public saving falls 40.
choices.feedback: The purchase PV increase is 150, causing C₁ to fall 60. Future taxes must cover the remaining PV burden of 130.

choices.text: ΔG₂=75, ΔT₂=125; both saving components are unchanged.
choices.feedback: This purchase path reduces C₁ by only 48, so national saving falls 12.

choices.text: ΔG₂=112.5, ΔT₂=112.5; national saving is unchanged and the budget balances.
choices.feedback: The current deficit rises 40, requiring another 50 in future taxes beyond future purchases.

st.explanation: Zero ΔS₁ requires −ΔC₁=ΔG₁=60. Thus 0.4(60+ΔG₂/1.25)=60, giving ΔG₂=112.5. The government requires ΔT₂=ΔG₂+R(ΔG₁−ΔT₁)=112.5+1.25(40)=162.5. ΔS_private=−20+60=40 and ΔS_public=20−60=−40.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 2, PDF pp10–22; original synthesis
st.rationale: Solves an inverse purchase-path problem and then a separate tax-financing problem with consistent dates.

st.prompt: In a hypothetical tax-timing survey, 43 households each receive a current withholding reduction of 200 and spend half of it. Another 57 each receive 1,000 and spend none. All relief is repaid through future taxes at equal present value. Current Y and G are fixed. What can the observed spending establish?

choices.text: The aggregate MPC is 50% because spenders spend half.
choices.feedback: This omits the larger relief received by nonspenders.

choices.text: National saving rises 61,300 because households save that much relief.
choices.feedback: That is private saving growth; public saving falls 65,600.

choices.text: Equal-PV repayment proves consumption must be unchanged, so the observations are impossible.
choices.feedback: Ricardian neutrality also needs household-level assumptions such as unrestricted finance; observed departures can test these assumptions.

choices.text: The observations identify borrowing constraints as the unique explanation.
choices.feedback: Several mechanisms, including horizon, incidence and expectations, could explain departures. This arithmetic does not uniquely identify one.

choices.text: Current aggregate consumption rises 4,300 and national saving falls 4,300; the amount-weighted spending share is 43/656, not 43%.
choices.feedback: Spending is 43×100, while relief totals 43×200+57×1,000=65,600. Head counts are not dollar weights.

choices.text: The aggregate MPC is 43% and national saving falls 28,208.
choices.feedback: The proportion of respondents who spend is not the fraction of total relief spent.

st.explanation: Total relief is 65,600, spending is 4,300 and private saving rises 61,300. Public saving falls 65,600, so national saving falls 4,300. The amount-weighted share is 4,300/65,600=43/656≈6.55%. The observation conflicts with universal exact neutrality in this experiment but does not isolate a single cause.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 2, PDF pp10–22; original synthesis; hypothetical data, not the lecture survey figures
st.rationale: Requires weighted aggregation, public-private reconciliation and a disciplined inference about evidence.

st.prompt: In a closed goods-market exercise, Y=1,000, C=800−0.5G₁−0.4G₂−200r and I=300−400r. The coefficients already summarize the household wealth response; treat them as fixed. Initially G₁=200 and G₂=250. Then G₁ rises 30 and G₂ rises 50. Which equilibrium change follows?

choices.text: r rises by 1/20 and I falls by 20.
choices.feedback: This counts the current purchase change but omits both consumption responses.

choices.text: r rises by 1/40 and I falls by 10.
choices.feedback: This includes the current wealth effect but omits the future purchase effect.

choices.text: r is unchanged because taxes can be retimed.
choices.feedback: The purchase path changes, so tax timing neutrality does not fix total demand.

choices.text: r falls by 1/120 and I falls by 10/3.
choices.feedback: Investment slopes downward in r, so a lower rate raises investment.

choices.text: The model cannot be solved because government purchases appear in consumption.
choices.feedback: The stated reduced-form consumption rule and goods identity form a complete linear equation.

choices.text: r falls by 1/120 and I rises by 10/3, despite higher current purchases.
choices.feedback: The two-date purchase change reduces consumption demand by 35 at fixed r, more than the 30 current purchase increase.

st.explanation: Initially total demand is 1,100−600r, so r=1/6. The shock changes its intercept by −0.5(30)−0.4(50)+30=−5. Hence Δr=−5/600=−1/120 and ΔI=−400Δr=10/3. The result uses the explicitly stated reduced form; it is not a claim that every fiscal expansion lowers rates.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 2, PDF pp10–22; original synthesis; original reduced-form equilibrium application
st.rationale: Requires combining dated wealth effects with an endogenous rate, reversing a familiar current-spending shortcut.

st.prompt: A worker has U=ln c₁+ln l₁+β(ln c₂+ln l₂), β=0.8, h=10, R=1.25, gross wages (2,4), no assets and unrestricted borrowing. Compare A: a lump-sum current tax of 10, with B: a 50% tax on current labor earnings and no lump-sum tax. These are alternative tax experiments, not equal-revenue policies. Which current labor outcomes and interpretation are correct?

choices.text: A: n₁=25/6. B: n₁=0, so B collects zero; equal rates or intended revenue do not establish Ricardian equivalence.
choices.feedback: A changes wealth at unchanged wage; B lowers the net wage to one and induces the current no-work corner.

choices.text: A and B both collect 10 and leave n₁ unchanged.
choices.feedback: The earnings tax base is chosen by the worker and is not the full time endowment.
This reverses the wealth and substitution effects of the two taxes.
The negative interior labor candidate under B is infeasible; impose n₁≥0.

choices.text: Both cases are neutral because the tax is current rather than future.
choices.feedback: Tax timing neutrality requires lump-sum taxes and unchanged relevant lifetime burdens, not merely a particular date.

choices.text: A raises the opportunity cost of leisure; B changes wealth only.
choices.feedback: A lump-sum tax leaves the wage price unchanged. The proportional earnings tax changes it.

st.explanation: A leaves full income 52−10=42: c₁=42/3.6=35/3, l₁=c₁/2=35/6 and n₁=25/6. B gives net wages (1,4), whose interior l₁ exceeds 10; the constrained optimum has no current work. B therefore raises no earnings-tax revenue. Labor responses must be evaluated before comparing fiscal receipts.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 2, PDF pp10–22; original synthesis; Tutorial 5 QP p1; original cross-model application
st.rationale: Uses household optimization to expose a tax-base feedback and explains why a tax-timing theorem cannot cover a distorted wage.

st.prompt: A firm maximizes Π=10√N₁−2N₁−2J+[0.75(12√K₂+8√N₂)−3N₂+1.6K₂]/1.1, with K₂=64+J and J≥0. Current capital survivors are 64; the output-revenue tax applies only next period. Which optimum and capital test are correct?

choices.feedback: The common future discount factor cancels from the future labor FOC; it does not multiply the optimal labor level.

choices.text: N₁=6.25, N₂=1, J=0; the after-tax MPK at K₂=64 is 0.5625<0.6.
choices.feedback: Labor FOCs are interior. The desired unconstrained K₂ is 56.25, below survivors, so irreversible investment is zero.
This is the unconstrained disinvestment amount and violates J≥0.

choices.text: N₁=6.25, N₂=1, J=−7.75; clipping K₂ to zero solves the constraint.
choices.feedback: The constraint is K₂≥64, not merely K₂≥0.
Future output is taxed, so the labor FOC is 0.75×4/√N₂=3.
K₂=100 follows from ignoring the output tax in the capital FOC.

st.explanation: Current labor: 5/√N₁=2 gives 6.25. Future labor: 0.75×4/√N₂=3 gives 1. Capital: −2+[0.75×6/√K₂+1.6]/1.1=0 gives a net output hurdle 2.2−1.6=0.6 and K₂=56.25. Since K₂ must be at least 64, J=0. At that boundary the derivative in the feasible increasing-J direction is negative, validating the corner.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 3, PDF pp12–41; original synthesis
st.rationale: Adds an investment irreversibility boundary to three separate FOCs, requiring a derivative check rather than blindly solving equalities.

st.prompt: A firm has MPK₂=30/√K₂, current capital K₁=100, depreciation d=0.2, purchase price q₁=10 and R=1.1. It cannot disinvest. Initially future resale price q₂=10 and a tax of 20% applies only to output revenue. Then q₂ rises to 12 while the output tax rises to 30%. What happens to actual gross physical investment?

choices.text: It remains zero because inherited capital is fixed.
choices.feedback: Inherited survivors are fixed, but the firm may add new capital.

choices.text: It rises from 0 to 225.
choices.feedback: 225 is the desired future stock. Subtract the 80 surviving units to obtain gross physical investment.

choices.text: It rises from 0 to 145, because the higher resale payoff more than offsets the tax increase.
choices.feedback: The pre-tax hurdles fall from 3.75 to 2, giving desired capital 64 then 225; survivors are 80.

choices.text: It falls because an output tax increase always dominates every other shock.
choices.feedback: Tax is only one component. The resale-price increase lowers the net user cost sharply.

choices.text: It rises from −16 to 145.
choices.feedback: The initial desired disinvestment is infeasible; actual initial investment is zero.

choices.text: It rises from 0 to 84.
choices.feedback: This does not solve the new MPK equation 30/√K₂=2.

st.explanation: The pre-tax hurdle is [Rq₁−(1−d)q₂]/(1−τ). Initially it is (11−8)/0.8=3.75, so K*=64<80 and actual J=0. Afterwards it is (11−9.6)/0.7=2, so K*=225 and J=225−80=145. This is the explicitly extended unequal-resale-price model.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 3, PDF pp12–41; original synthesis
st.rationale: Combines opposed tax and resale shocks with a switch from constrained to unconstrained capital adjustment.

st.prompt: Consider a divisible capital investment with q₁=5, R=1.1, d=0.1 and expected resale q₂=7. Future output is 20√K, with no output tax. Capital is the only choice. What does the model predict first with K≥0 only, then with an added capacity bound K≤100?

choices.text: K=156.25 both before and after the bound.
choices.feedback: This result incorrectly takes the absolute value of the negative hurdle and also violates the capacity bound.

choices.text: Every K is equally profitable when user cost is nonpositive.
choices.feedback: Here user cost is strictly negative and MPK is positive, so the objective strictly rises.

choices.text: The ordinary common-price rule gives the valid answer K=100.
choices.feedback: That rule ignores q₂≠q₁. The bounded answer happens to be 100, but requires the boundary argument.

choices.text: No finite unconstrained maximum; with the capacity bound, K=100.
choices.feedback: Net user cost is 5.5−6.3=−0.8. Output and resale together make the objective strictly increasing, including at the capacity boundary.

choices.text: A finite interior optimum solves 10/√K=0.8.
choices.feedback: The user cost is negative, not positive. Positive MPK cannot equal −0.8.

choices.text: K=0 in both cases because resale exceeds purchase cost.
choices.feedback: The large resale payoff makes investment more attractive, not less.

st.explanation: The incremental objective is −5K+[20√K+6.3K]/1.1. Its derivative is [10/√K+0.8]/1.1>0 for K>0. As K grows, the positive linear resale-financing spread makes value unbounded. Adding K≤100 yields a maximum at 100. A negative user-cost output is a model-limit warning, not permission to square away its sign.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 3, PDF pp12–41; original synthesis
st.rationale: Diagnoses nonexistence of an interior solution and then solves a changed feasible set instead of forcing a familiar MPK intersection.

st.prompt: A reversible firm can buy or sell capital at unit price. Its MPK is 2/√K₂, r=0.1 and K₁=600. Depreciation rises from 0.1 to 0.2. Negative gross physical investment means selling capital; it is permitted here. Which comparison is correct?

choices.text: Gross investment rises by 60 and desired capital stays fixed.
choices.feedback: Depreciation also raises user cost and lowers the desired stock.

choices.text: Gross investment is zero in both cases because negative investment is forbidden.
choices.feedback: The prompt explicitly permits reversible capital sales; irreversibility is a different model.

choices.text: Net investment rises because gross investment rises.
choices.feedback: Net investment is K₂−K₁ and follows the falling desired stock, not the replacement adjustment.

choices.text: Gross investment becomes positive after depreciation rises.
choices.feedback: It changes from −440 to −3920/9, both negative.

choices.text: Desired K₂ falls by 500/9, but gross investment rises by 40/9 and remains negative.
choices.feedback: The desired stock falls from 100 to 400/9, while surviving inherited capital falls by 60.

choices.text: Gross investment falls by 500/9, exactly like the desired stock.
choices.feedback: This omits the change in surviving inherited capital.

st.explanation: Initial user cost is 0.2, so K₂=(2/0.2)²=100 and J=100−0.9(600)=−440. New user cost is 0.3, so K₂=400/9 and J=400/9−480=−3920/9. Thus ΔK₂=−500/9 but ΔJ=40/9. The result concerns a reversible firm, not an assertion that aggregate production of new capital is negative.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 3, PDF pp12–41; original synthesis
st.rationale: Constructs a concrete counterexample to a one-direction depreciation rule, keeping stock changes, surviving capital and reversible flows distinct.

st.prompt: One unit of capital costs 10 now, produces 2.25 extra output next period and has an untaxed salvage value of 8. R=1.25. Compare A: an immediate investment credit of 2; B: a deduction of 10 against other taxable income next period, at a 20% tax rate. Both incentives are fully usable; this project’s output is otherwise untaxed. Which investment decision is correct?

choices.text: Accept under both because each incentive has face value 2.
choices.feedback: Equal face values at different dates do not have equal present value.

choices.text: Reject under both because MPK is below r+d.
choices.feedback: The stated monetary costs and salvage must be valued; a unit-price shortcut is not applicable.

choices.text: Reject under A and accept under B because deductions reduce income.
choices.feedback: The later deduction is less valuable than the equally sized immediate credit.

choices.text: A and B both reduce the MPK hurdle to 0.5.
choices.feedback: This incorrectly subtracts the whole deduction or mixes current and future units.

choices.text: Accept under B only if the tax saving is taxed again at 20%.
choices.feedback: The prompt specifies a usable tax reduction of 2; taxing it again has no basis and would reduce value further.

choices.text: Accept under A, reject under B: the MPK hurdles are 2 and 2.5 respectively.
choices.feedback: The credit cuts current cost to 8. The deduction gives a future tax saving of 2, worth only 1.6 today.

st.explanation: Under A, −8+(MPK+8)/1.25≥0 requires MPK≥2. Under B, −10+(MPK+8+2)/1.25≥0 requires MPK≥2.5. The actual MPK 2.25 lies between them. NPVs are +0.2 under A and −0.2 under B. Timing and the tax base matter even when both headline incentives appear to be two units.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 3, PDF pp12–41; original synthesis
st.rationale: Requires deriving incentive cash flows, aligning dates and testing a marginal project against two different hurdles.

st.prompt: Future output is 12√K₂+8√N₂. The firm pays unit capital price, has r=0.25, d=0.15 and untaxed salvage (1−d)K₂. Future wage falls from 4 to 2; all other terms remain fixed. There are no binding constraints. Which result is correct?

choices.text: N₂ rises from 1 to 4, K₂ stays 225 and optimized firm PV rises 3.2.
choices.feedback: The wage changes the separable labor component, not MPK. The future labor surplus rises from 4 to 8.

choices.text: N₂ rises from 1 to 4 and K₂ rises because total profits rise.
choices.feedback: Higher total profits do not by themselves change the marginal return to capital in this separable technology.

choices.text: N₂ doubles to 2, K₂ stays 225 and PV rises 1.6.
choices.feedback: The labor FOC 4/√N=w gives a squared wage response, not a proportional one.

choices.text: N₂ rises from 1 to 4, K₂ stays 225 and PV rises 4.
choices.feedback: Four is the future surplus gain; its current value is 4/1.25.

choices.text: N₂ rises to 6.25 because future wages must be discounted separately.
choices.feedback: The future wage and future marginal output share the same discount factor, which cancels.

choices.text: K₂ falls because lower labor cost increases the user cost of capital.
choices.feedback: Neither the capital purchase price, depreciation nor financing return changes.

st.explanation: Labor satisfies 4/√N₂=w₂, yielding 1 then 4. Capital satisfies 6/√K₂=r+d=0.4, giving K₂=225 in both cases. Optimized future labor surplus is initially 8−4=4 and then 16−8=8, so PV rises by (8−4)/1.25=3.2. The absence of a capital effect depends on the stated additive technology.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 3, PDF pp12–41; original synthesis
st.rationale: Uses a full optimized profit change to test whether a total-profit improvement really shifts the capital marginal condition.

st.prompt: Initially Sᵈ=50+200r and Iᵈ=140−400r. Later, saving shifts left by a and investment shifts right by b at every r. The observed equilibrium changes from (r,I)=(0.15,80) to (0.20,70). Infer a and b. If r were instead held at 0.15 after those shifts while Y stayed fixed, what unintended inventory change would reconcile actual saving and investment?

choices.text: The two observed equilibria cannot identify both shifts.
choices.feedback: With both original slopes known, each observed curve equation separately identifies its intercept change.

choices.text: a=20, b=10; unintended inventory investment is −30.
choices.feedback: The new saving intercept is 30 and investment intercept 150. At r=.15, desired S=60 and I=90, so inventories must fall by 30.

choices.text: a=10, b=20; unintended inventories rise 30.
choices.feedback: Substituting the observed equilibrium gives the opposite intercept shifts, and excess spending reduces inventories.

choices.text: a=20, b=10; unintended inventories rise 30.
choices.feedback: Desired spending exceeds output when Iᵈ>Sᵈ, so inventory accumulation is negative.

choices.text: a=20, b=−10; inventories are unchanged.
choices.feedback: The new investment equation must satisfy 70=140+b−400(.20), requiring b=10.

choices.text: a=0, b=30; actual S≠I by 30.
choices.feedback: The saving observation requires a left shift, and actual accounting equality includes unintended inventories.

st.explanation: At the new point, 70=50−a+40 gives a=20, and 70=140+b−80 gives b=10. At the old rate, Sᵈ=30+30=60 and Iᵈ=150−60=90. With unchanged output, excess desired spending draws inventories down by 30; actual investment is 90−30=60, matching saving. Desired disequilibrium does not break an accounting identity.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 3, PDF pp12–41; original synthesis
st.rationale: Infers hidden shifts from equilibrium observations, then switches to disequilibrium and reconstructs actual inventory accounting.

st.prompt: At fixed Y, desired saving is initially vertical at 100 and Iᵈ=180−400r. Current G then rises 40, reducing C by 10 through its wealth effect. At the same time, an innovation shifts investment demand right by 50. Saving remains rate-insensitive. Which final outcome is correct?

choices.text: I=70 and r=0.20 because vertical saving fixes the interest rate.
choices.feedback: Vertical saving fixes quantity, while r adjusts to make desired investment equal that quantity.

choices.text: I=100 and r=0.325 because the innovation offsets fiscal crowding out.
choices.feedback: The innovation changes the clearing rate, but cannot restore saving under the stated vertical supply closure.

choices.text: I=70 and r=0.40; realized investment falls 30 although investment demand shifted right.
choices.feedback: The fiscal shock reduces national saving by 40−10=30. The new investment equation is 230−400r.

choices.text: I=150 and r=0.20 because innovation adds 50 to investment.
choices.feedback: This evaluates the shifted investment curve at the old rate without clearing the reduced saving supply.

choices.text: I=60 and r=0.425 because G crowds out I one for one.
choices.feedback: Consumption falls 10, so national saving falls only 30, not 40.

choices.text: I=120 and r=0.275 because the two shifts net to +20.
choices.feedback: Shifts on different curves cannot be added directly to equilibrium investment when saving is vertical.

st.explanation: Initially 100=180−400r gives r=.20. The fiscal shock changes S by −ΔC−ΔG=10−40=−30, so new S=70. New Iᵈ=230−400r; equating it to 70 gives r=.40. Innovation raises desired investment at each rate but the saving constraint pins realized equilibrium investment at 70.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 3, PDF pp12–41; original synthesis
st.rationale: Combines a wealth-adjusted fiscal shock, an investment shift and a limiting supply slope to separate demand from realized equilibrium.

st.prompt: A firm has MPK₂=30/√K₂, K₁=40, r=.1 and d=.2. Purchase and future resale prices are equal within each scenario. Initially pₖ=10 and the tax on output revenue is 20%. They change to pₖ=8 and tax 36%; purchase and salvage are untaxed. Which statement about desired capital and gross investment is correct?

choices.text: Physical J falls from 320 to 256.
choices.feedback: Those are expenditures pₖJ, not quantities of capital goods.

choices.text: K₂ stays 64 and physical J stays 24.
choices.feedback: Surviving capital is (1−.2)40=32, so the required addition is 64−32=32.

choices.text: The user cost itself stays 3.75.
choices.feedback: The user cost falls from 3 to 2.4. The tax-adjusted pre-tax MPK hurdle remains 3.75.

choices.text: K₂ stays 64 and physical J stays 32, while real investment expenditure falls from 320 to 256.
choices.feedback: Both pre-tax MPK hurdles equal 3.75, so the physical stock and flow are unchanged. Their purchase price falls 20%.

choices.text: K₂ falls because the output tax rate rises.
choices.feedback: The lower capital price exactly offsets the tax change in the pre-tax hurdle.

choices.text: K₂ rises because the capital price falls.
choices.feedback: That ignores the reduced retained output share.

st.explanation: Initial hurdle is (.1+.2)10/(1−.2)=3.75. New hurdle is (.1+.2)8/(1−.36)=3.75. Therefore K₂=(30/3.75)²=64 in both cases. Survivors are 32, so J=32, whereas spending pₖJ is 320 then 256. Equal desired capital does not imply equal investment expenditure when its price changes.
st.source: Lecture 3 part 3, PDF pp12–41; original synthesis
st.rationale: Requires recognizing an exact offset in tax-adjusted incentives and distinguishing physical stocks, physical flows and expenditure.

st.prompt: Real money demand is L=500+Y−1,000i, Y=800 and target P=2. Contracts target a 10% real return using the exact Fisher equation under a single anticipated inflation rate. Expected inflation rises from 20% to 30%. The central bank accommodates money demand to preserve P. Actual inflation on the new contract later equals 50%. What are the new nominal M and realized real return?

choices.text: M=1,740 and realized r=10%.
choices.feedback: Ten percent was the conditional target; actual inflation differs from the anticipated value.

choices.text: M=1,960 and realized r=−4.67%.
choices.feedback: 1,960 is the old money supply at i=.32. Money demand changes when the nominal rate rises.

choices.text: M=2,180 and realized r=−4.67%.
choices.feedback: Higher nominal opportunity cost reduces desired money, so accommodating M falls rather than rises.

choices.text: M=870 and realized r=−7%.
choices.feedback: 870 is real balances. Nominal M multiplies by P=2, and exact real return divides the nominal gross return by 1.5.

choices.text: M=1,740 and realized r=−7/150, approximately −4.67%.
choices.feedback: The new nominal contract rate is 43%; money demand is 870. Its realized gross real return is 1.43/1.50.

choices.text: M=1,800 and realized r=−10%.
choices.feedback: This uses i=r+πᵉ instead of exact Fisher and then subtracts actual inflation.

st.explanation: Initially 1+i=1.1×1.2=1.32 and M=2(1,300−320)=1,960. Afterwards 1+i=1.1×1.3=1.43 and M=2(1,300−430)=1,740. Ex post, r=1.43/1.50−1=−7/150. Money accommodation here holds the real return target and price level fixed; it is not the fixed-M/P experiment in which nominal i is pinned instead.
st.source: Lecture 4, PDF pp20–43; Lecture 4A, PDF pp6–8; original synthesis
st.rationale: Combines exact contract pricing, endogenous money accommodation and an ex-post inflation surprise with explicit closures.

st.prompt: Real money demand follows L=kY^0.5 i^−0.25 with positive Y and i and constant k. Over a finite interval, Y rises 21%, i rises 46.41%, and nominal M rises 10%. Compare exact inflation from M/P=L with the initial-point first-order growth approximation. Which pair is correct?

choices.text: Both exact and approximate inflation are 11.1025%.
choices.feedback: The elasticity formula in simple percentage changes is a local approximation, not an exact finite-change identity.

choices.text: Exact inflation is −1.1025%; approximate inflation is 10%.
choices.feedback: The negative number is the approximate demand growth, not inflation.

choices.text: Exact inflation is 0%; approximate inflation is 1.1025%.
choices.feedback: Constant real demand does not eliminate the effect of 10% nominal money growth.

choices.text: Exact inflation is 10%; the approximation is −11.1025%.
choices.feedback: Inflation subtracts demand growth from money growth; the signs have been reversed.

choices.text: Exact inflation is 31%; the approximation is 10%.
choices.feedback: A 21% income change does not translate one-for-one into money demand, and the rate effect offsets it exactly here.

choices.text: Exact inflation is 10%; the first-order approximation is 11.1025%.
choices.feedback: Real demand changes by √1.21/(1.4641)^0.25=1. Its first-order proportional change is .5(.21)−.25(.4641)=−.011025.

st.explanation: The chosen gross changes are 1.21=1.1² and 1.4641=1.1⁴. Thus L₁/L₀=1.1/1.1=1 and P₁/P₀=1.1. The first-order formula yields π≈.10−.5(.21)−(−.25)(.4641)=.111025. Constant elasticities make log changes exact, but do not make large simple-percentage changes additive.
st.source: Lecture 4, PDF pp20–43; Lecture 4A, PDF pp6–8; original synthesis
st.rationale: Distinguishes exact nonlinear growth factors, constant elasticities and a local approximation in an offsetting joint shock.

st.prompt: A stable affine money demand is L=a+bY+ci. Holding i fixed, ΔY=40 raises L by 40. Holding Y fixed, Δi=.02 lowers L by 30. At Y=600 and i=.04, L=900. Next, Y=660 and i=0. To hold P=2, what M is needed, and what happens if i then rises to .01 while P and Y remain fixed?

choices.text: M=2,040 initially, then M=2,010; a zero point interest elasticity at i=0 does not imply zero level sensitivity.
choices.feedback: The experiments identify b=1 and c=−1,500, then a=360. L at the boundary is 1,020 and subsequently 1,005.

choices.text: M=2,040 at both rates because the initial interest elasticity is zero.
choices.feedback: The elasticity multiplies i, but the level derivative c remains −1,500.

choices.text: M=1,020 initially, then M=1,005.
choices.feedback: These are real balances; nominal M must multiply by P=2.

choices.text: M=1,800 initially, then M=1,770.
choices.feedback: This carries the old demand level into a state with changed income and rate.

choices.text: M=2,040 initially, then M=2,340.
choices.feedback: A one-percentage-point increase means Δi=.01, giving ΔL=−15, not +150.

choices.text: No answer exists because percentage growth in i from zero is undefined.
choices.feedback: The original level function remains well-defined and avoids the undefined growth ratio.

st.explanation: b=40/40=1 and c=−30/.02=−1,500. Initial information gives a=900−600+60=360. New L=360+660=1,020 and M=2,040. Raising i to .01 lowers L by 15, requiring M=2,010 at P=2. At i=0, η_i=ci/L=0, but one cannot multiply it by an undefined percentage rate change.
st.source: Lecture 4, PDF pp20–43; Lecture 4A, PDF pp6–8; original synthesis
st.rationale: Identifies a demand equation from experiments, then handles a zero-rate boundary without an invalid elasticity shortcut.

st.prompt: A closed asset exercise contains a fixed nominal money stock of 200 and one tradable zero-coupon bond paying 1,000 next period. Its current price is q. Desired money is 30% of current total financial wealth W=200+q; desired bond holdings take the rest. Treat this portfolio rule as given. Starting from q=800, what q and bond yield clear the asset markets, allowing wealth to be revalued?

choices.text: q=200 and yield=400%.
choices.feedback: A price equal to the money stock is not implied by portfolio shares; desired money would be only 120.

choices.text: q=1,400/3 and yield=8/7, about 114.29%.
choices.feedback: Clearing requires 200=.3(200+q). The lower bond price also lowers financial wealth, so its initial value cannot be held fixed.

choices.text: q=700 and yield=3/7.
choices.feedback: Subtracting the initial excess demand for money once ignores the change in desired money when bond wealth is revalued.

choices.text: q=800 and yield=25%.
choices.feedback: At q=800, desired money is 300, above the fixed supply 200.

choices.text: q=1,000 and yield=0%.
choices.feedback: At par, desired money is 360, so the asset allocation does not clear.

choices.text: q=1,400/3 and yield=7/8.
choices.feedback: The yield is payoff divided by purchase price minus one: 1,000/(1,400/3)−1=8/7.

st.explanation: Solve 200=.3(200+q) to obtain q=1,400/3. Total wealth is 2,000/3, and desired bond value .7W=1,400/3 equals supply value q. The yield is 1,000/q−1=8/7. Initial excess money demand induces bond selling and a lower price, but the final condition must use the revalued wealth.
st.source: Lecture 4, PDF pp20–43; Lecture 4A, PDF pp6–8; original synthesis; original portfolio-rule illustration
st.rationale: Requires solving asset valuation and desired wealth shares jointly, then checking Walras consistency and the price-yield conversion.

st.prompt: In an illustrative statistical revision, old M1=500 and M2=1,000. Savings deposits of 200, already in M2, are newly included in M1. Next, households move 20 from an M2-only retail money-market fund into currency. Nominal GDP remains 2,000; no new deposits or currency are created overall. What follows?

choices.text: New M1=720, so P must rise 44% by the quantity identity.
choices.feedback: Velocity is not held fixed, and the identity alone does not provide that causal conclusion.

choices.text: New M1=720 and velocity=9/25.
choices.feedback: Velocity is nominal GDP divided by the chosen money stock, not its reciprocal.

choices.text: New M1=720, M2=1,000 and M1 velocity=25/9; the 44% M1 rise does not establish a 44% monetary injection or inflation.
choices.feedback: Reclassification adds 200 to the narrow measure, and the within-M2 portfolio move adds another 20. M2 is unchanged.

choices.text: New M1=720 and M2=1,220; velocity is unchanged.
choices.feedback: M2 already contained both the reclassified deposits and the fund units, so adding them again double-counts.

choices.text: New M1=700, M2=980 and velocity=20/7.
choices.feedback: The fund-to-currency transfer raises M1 and leaves M2 unchanged.

choices.text: New M1=500 and M2=1,000 because no money was printed.
choices.feedback: Measured aggregates can change through definition and composition without new issuance.

st.explanation: M1 becomes 500+200+20=720. M2 remains 1,000 because both operations occur within its unchanged membership. Measured M1 velocity becomes 2,000/720=25/9, down from 4. Interpreting a definitional or compositional rise as new purchasing power would confuse measurement with a policy shock.
st.source: Lecture 4, PDF pp20–43; Lecture 4A, PDF pp6–8; original synthesis; Lecture 4 monetary-aggregate discussion; hypothetical revision
st.rationale: Combines nested aggregate accounting, reclassification, portfolio substitution and a false causal use of an identity.

st.prompt: Compare three separate flexible-price states with fixed Y and r=.02, money demand L=150−1,000i and i≈r+πᵉ. Initially M=200 and πᵉ=.03. News raises πᵉ to .06 with M unchanged. At shipment, M becomes 260 and πᵉ falls to .02. Which price path and interpretation are correct?

choices.text: P: 2 → 20/7 → 26/11; the final price is below its initial level.
choices.feedback: 26/11≈2.364 is below the news price but above the initial 2.

choices.text: P must rise at both transitions because more money is always inflationary.
choices.feedback: That comparison holds other determinants fixed; here expected inflation and money demand also change.
These invert M/L; equilibrium is P=M/L, not L/M.

choices.text: P: 2 → 20/7 → 26/11; the shipment state has a lower P than the news state despite more nominal money.
choices.feedback: The fall in expected inflation raises real money demand from 70 to 110, more than offsetting 30% money growth relative to the news state.

choices.text: P: 2 → 2 → 2.6; prices can only respond when M changes.
choices.feedback: Expected inflation changes current desired real balances before the shipment.

choices.text: P: 2 → 20/7 → 26/7; demand remains 70 after shipment.
choices.feedback: The final expected inflation rate changes i and money demand again.

st.explanation: Initial i=.05 gives L=100 and P=2. News gives i=.08, L=70 and P=20/7. At shipment i=.04, L=110 and P=26/11. Relative to news, P changes by (26/11)/(20/7)−1=−19/110≈−17.27%. These are conditional comparative states with specified expectations, not a fully solved dynamic expectation path.
st.source: Lecture 4, PDF pp20–43; Lecture 4A, PDF pp6–8; original synthesis; Tutorial 6 Q3; original three-state comparison
st.rationale: Separates news from issuance, compares two simultaneous determinants and avoids treating a conditional exercise as a solved dynamic model.

st.prompt: Initially M=100 and P=1. Compare two alternative one-period monetary-financing experiments from that same starting point. A prints 50 and ends with real money demand 80. B prints 100 and ends with real money demand 60. All new money is spent on goods at each experiment’s final clearing price. Which real revenue comparison is correct?

choices.text: A finances 80 goods and B finances 60, so more issuance reduces revenue here.
choices.feedback: Those are the final real money stocks, including previously existing money, not the government’s new-money spending.

choices.text: A finances 80/3 goods and B finances 30; real revenue rises 100%.
A finances 50/80 goods and B finances 100/60.
choices.feedback: Real demand is not the price level. First use P=M/L.

choices.text: No financing comparison can be made without a stable demand elasticity.
choices.feedback: The final real-demand quantities and the spending timing are supplied, so direct stock and price accounting suffices.

choices.text: A finances 80/3 goods; B finances 30 goods. Doubling issuance raises real revenue only 12.5%.
choices.feedback: Final prices are 150/80=1.875 and 200/60=10/3, so divide each new issue by its own final price.

choices.text: A finances 50 goods and B finances 100, exactly doubling revenue.
choices.feedback: This values spending at the initial price despite the specified final-price timing.

st.explanation: Under A, P=150/80=15/8 and real new-money spending is 50/(15/8)=80/3. Under B, P=200/60=10/3 and real spending is 100/(10/3)=30. The increase is (30−80/3)/(80/3)=1/8. This illustration shows how demand flight and price adjustment can erode the real yield of monetary finance; the given demand responses are assumptions, not estimated laws.
st.source: Lecture 4, PDF pp20–43; Lecture 4A, PDF pp6–8; original synthesis
st.rationale: Connects money-demand flight, price clearing and a carefully dated government resource flow, distinguishing new issuance from total balances.

st.prompt: A bond is bought for 100, pays a coupon of 8 over the year and is then sold for 96 just after that coupon. The price level rose 10%. At that sale date the bond has one final coupon of 8 plus redemption of 100 due next year. What are the seller’s realized nominal and real returns, and the new buyer’s one-year yield if held to maturity?

choices.feedback: This uses coupon rates while omitting the seller’s capital loss, exact inflation adjustment and the buyer’s discounted price.
The nominal and buyer-yield figures are right, but the exact real return is 1.04/1.10−1.
This swaps the seller’s completed holding period with the new buyer’s future contract.
The buyer’s payoff includes both the final coupon and redemption, not only the four-unit capital gain.
The seller’s capital loss is four, but the coupon of eight makes the total nominal return positive four.
The seller receives 8+96 against 100. The buyer instead pays 96 for a future payoff of 108.

st.explanation: The seller’s nominal total return is (8+96−100)/100=.04. The exact real return is 1.04/1.10−1=−6/110. At the sale date, the new buyer’s yield is (108−96)/96=.125. A negative realized real return does not imply a negative nominal holding-period return, and the new quoted yield concerns a different price and interval.
st.source: Lecture 4, PDF pp20–43; Lecture 4A, PDF pp6–8; original synthesis
st.rationale: Separates three commonly conflated returns across two investors, two holding intervals and exact inflation adjustment.

st.prompt: Nominal money stocks at quarters 0–7 are 100,102,108,117,119,120,127,137. Real GDP at quarters 1–7 is 100,101,105,108,104,101,103. Define money growth in quarter t as 100(Mₜ/Mₜ₋₁−1), using the immediately preceding stock as the denominator. Compare the strict interior turning points of money growth with those of real GDP. Which conclusion is supported?

choices.text: Money growth peaks in quarter 3 and troughs in 5, leading the matching GDP turns by one quarter; the rising money stock and these timing facts do not establish causality
choices.feedback: Growth turns must be computed from dated stock ratios; GDP peaks in 4 and troughs in 6.

choices.text: The money stock falls before both GDP contractions, identifying money as the cause
choices.feedback: Every supplied stock observation rises, and timing alone does not identify a causal innovation.

choices.text: Money growth peaks in quarter 3 and troughs in 5, so it lags GDP by one quarter
choices.feedback: A quarter-3 turn occurs before the matching quarter-4 turn, so the direction of timing is reversed.

choices.text: Money growth and GDP have coincident turns in quarters 4 and 6
choices.feedback: Quarters 4 and 6 are the GDP turns; the growth-rate series turns one quarter earlier.

choices.text: Quarter-3 money growth is 9%, its peak, and the GDP peak follows in quarter 4
choices.feedback: Nine is the stock increase, not its percentage growth: the rate is 100(117−108)/108=8⅓%.

choices.text: The computed one-quarter lead proves that an exogenous money expansion causes the later output expansion
choices.feedback: Anticipation, accommodation or common determinants can generate a lead without the stated causal effect.

st.explanation: The seven growth rates are approximately 2,5.882,8.333,1.709,0.840,5.833,7.874 percent. Their strict interior peak and trough occur in quarters 3 and 5. GDP peaks in 4 and troughs in 6, so the matching turns have a one-quarter money-growth lead. The money stock itself never falls; its level is a different series from its growth rate. The observations do not isolate an exogenous monetary shock.
st.source: Lecture 5, business-cycle series and timing; Tutorial 7 Q2, ANS pp2–4; Lecture 7, money causality debate
st.rationale: Requires constructing a growth series from stocks, using dated denominators, matching two types of turning points and separating predictive timing from causality.

st.prompt: At dates t=0,1,2,3, real activity is 98,101,102,104. A candidate trend is Tₜ=100+gt, where g>0 is unknown, and the cycle is the absolute gap activity−Tt. Find the exact set of g for which every activity observation is strictly below trend, the gap has a strict local peak at date 1 and a strict local trough at date 2. What also follows for the raw-activity growth-phase classification?

choices.text: 1<g<2; raw activity is an expansion throughout
choices.feedback: The turning conditions hold, but some values in this interval put the final observation on or above trend.

choices.text: 4/3≤g≤2; raw activity is an expansion throughout
choices.feedback: At the lower endpoint the final gap is zero; at the upper endpoint the last two gaps tie, violating strictness.

choices.text: 4/3<g<3; raw activity contracts between dates 1 and 2
choices.feedback: A trough at date 2 additionally requires g<2, and raw activity rises from 101 to 102.

choices.text: g>2; a negative gap is sufficient to establish the stipulated trough
choices.feedback: The final gap then does not rise after date 2, so the required local trough fails.

choices.text: No such g exists because activity cannot expand while all its gaps are negative
choices.feedback: A rising series can remain below a faster-growing trend, and its gap can have turns absent from the raw series.

choices.text: 4/3<g<2; raw activity is an expansion throughout even though all four gaps are negative
choices.feedback: Intersect the strict below-trend and strict turning-point inequalities; rising raw activity is a separate criterion.

st.explanation: The gaps are −2,1−g,2−2g,4−3g. All are negative exactly when g>4/3. Their consecutive changes are 3−g,1−g,2−g. A strict peak at date 1 requires the first change positive and second negative; a strict trough at date 2 requires the second negative and third positive. Together these give 1<g<2, hence the intersection 4/3<g<2. Raw activity rises at every transition regardless of g, so the growth-phase convention calls the whole observed path an expansion.
st.source: Tutorial 7 Q2, ANS pp2–4; Lecture 5, trend and turning points
st.rationale: An inverse trend problem requires intersecting three distinct strict inequalities and distinguishing turns of the gap from growth of the observed level.

st.prompt: Study A finds that money growth precedes output growth, without identifying the source of either change. Study B isolates an unexpected exogenous money-level increase while real fundamentals are unchanged, and finds a temporary output increase with prices initially fixed. Which joint conclusion follows?

choices.text: Both studies prove that productivity never drives cycles
choices.feedback: Neither excludes productive shocks in other episodes.

choices.text: B is predicted by a strict model with immediate neutrality and unchanged real fundamentals
choices.feedback: That benchmark has no temporary real response under its stated assumptions.

choices.text: A is incompatible with endogenous money responding to anticipated real activity
choices.feedback: Such an anticipation or accommodation mechanism is a possible alternative explanation.

choices.text: B proves every fiscal intervention raises welfare
choices.feedback: A monetary output response does not establish fiscal welfare effects.

choices.text: A alone does not identify monetary causality; B conflicts with the strict full-information flexible-price neutrality benchmark but does not uniquely prove efficiency wages
choices.feedback: The controlled shock tests a maintained benchmark, while several nominal-rigidity mechanisms could fit the response.

choices.text: A proves monetary causality and B proves efficiency wages uniquely
choices.feedback: Predictive timing is not causal identification, and B does not isolate a labor mechanism.

st.explanation: A can reflect anticipation, accommodation or omitted common determinants. B provides a stronger test because its nominal innovation and unchanged real fundamentals are stipulated. Its output response rejects the joint strict-neutrality assumptions for that setting, while leaving multiple rigidity or information mechanisms possible.
st.source: Lecture 5, facts and theory; Lecture 7, RBC debate and neutrality; Lecture 8, nominal rigidity
st.rationale: Requires distinguishing predictive evidence, a controlled counterfactual, a joint-hypothesis rejection and mechanism identification.

st.prompt: Numerical interest and inflation rates are measured in percentage points in this linear teaching model. At fixed P=2, C=25+0.5Y−3r, I=40−2r and L=Y−10r. Initially G=10,M=100, giving Y=100,r=5. The authority wants exactly Y=112,r=4 by changing G and M only. What policy pair is required?

choices.text: ΔG=0 and ΔM=+40
choices.feedback: That yields Y=110,r=4, missing the output target.

choices.text: ΔG=+1 and ΔM=+22
choices.feedback: The real-balance increase is 22, but nominal M must increase by P times that amount.

choices.text: ΔG=−1 and ΔM=−44
choices.feedback: Both required policy directions are reversed.

choices.text: ΔG=+1 and ΔM=+44
choices.feedback: At the target, C=69,I=32, so G=11; L=72 requires M=144.

choices.text: ΔG=+6 and ΔM=+24
choices.feedback: These do not satisfy the target resource identity or target money demand.

choices.text: ΔG=+12 and ΔM=0
choices.feedback: This ignores induced private spending and the desired balance change.

st.explanation: Work backward from the two targets rather than applying one policy multiplier. C=25+56−12=69 and I=40−8=32. Goods balance requires G=112−101=11. Real demand is 112−40=72, so M=2×72=144.
st.source: Lecture 6, IS–LM equilibrium; Tutorial 7 Q1; Tutorial 8 policy comparisons
st.rationale: An inverse two-instrument problem requires simultaneous goods, portfolio and unit-consistency checks.

st.prompt: Numerical interest and inflation rates are measured in percentage points in this linear teaching model. At fixed P, initially C=25+0.5Y−3r, I=40−2r,G=10, and real supply R=50 equals L=Y−10r. A wealth change raises autonomous consumption by 6 and autonomous real money demand by 20. Which new (Y,r,C) follows when both channels operate?

choices.feedback: This counts the autonomous consumption increase twice.
The net output and rate effects have been assigned the wrong signs.
The LM shift dominates output and the higher rate more than offsets the direct consumption gain.
This omits the autonomous money-demand increase.
This applies only the money-demand channel and omits the consumption change.
Output does not stay fixed for these magnitudes.

st.explanation: New IS is r=16.2−0.1Y. New money balance is 50=20+Y−10r, or r=0.1Y−3. Equating gives Y=96,r=6.6. Then C=31+48−19.8=59.2 and I=26.8. Despite a positive direct wealth effect, equilibrium C is below its original 60.
st.source: Lecture 6, IS and LM wealth shifters; Tutorial 7 Q1
st.rationale: Combines opposing wealth channels and derives an equilibrium consumption reversal, beyond naming ambiguous output effects.

st.prompt: Numerical interest and inflation rates are measured in percentage points in this linear teaching model. Both economies have goods balance Y=150−10r and R=50. Economy A has L=50+Y−20r. Economy B has L=50+0.5Y−10r. Their initial LM curves coincide at r=0.05Y, with Y=100,r=5. Each receives ΔR=15. Which comparison is correct?

choices.text: A must have a steeper initial LM than B
choices.feedback: Both have k/h=0.05 and the same intercept.

choices.text: A reaches Y=105,r=4.5; B reaches Y=110,r=4, despite identical initial LM curves
choices.feedback: The same slope does not identify how a fixed real-balance change moves its intercept.

choices.text: Both reach Y=105,r=4.5 because the initial slopes match
choices.feedback: Money-demand coefficients determine different vertical shifts from ΔR.

choices.text: Both reach Y=110,r=4 because the initial intersections match
choices.feedback: An identical initial equilibrium does not identify policy derivatives.

choices.text: A reaches Y=110,r=4 and B reaches Y=105,r=4.5
choices.feedback: The two monetary multipliers are reversed.

choices.text: Both remain at Y=100 because autonomous money demand is positive
choices.feedback: An additive intercept does not eliminate monetary transmission.

st.explanation: In A, the monetary multiplier is 10/(20+10)=1/3, so output rises 5. In B it is 10/(10+5)=2/3, so output rises 10. Their initial graph is identical, but ΔR/h lowers the intercept by different amounts. Use IS for the new rates.
st.source: Tutorial 8, ANS pp1–4; Lecture 6, money-demand sensitivity
st.rationale: Constructs observationally identical baseline diagrams with different policy responses and requires identifying the hidden parameter difference.

st.prompt: Numerical interest and inflation rates are measured in percentage points in this linear teaching model. The model is Y=A−10r and R=kY−hr with k,h>0. In separate experiments, ΔA=30 at fixed R raises Y by 20, while ΔR=12 at fixed A raises Y by 4. What parameters and LM slope are jointly implied?

choices.text: k=1,h=20 and slope 0.05
choices.feedback: The two multipliers identify h/10=2 and the common denominator 30.

choices.text: k=0.5,h=10 and slope 0.05
choices.feedback: This matches the fiscal ratio but predicts twice the observed monetary response.

choices.text: k=2,h=20 and slope 0.1
choices.feedback: It gives a fiscal multiplier of one-half rather than two-thirds.

choices.text: k=1,h=10 and slope 0.1
choices.feedback: Both implied multipliers disagree with the observations.

choices.text: k=20,h=1 and slope 20
choices.feedback: This exchanges behavioral coefficients and fails both experiments.

choices.text: Only the slope is identified, so infinitely many k,h pairs fit both experiments
choices.feedback: Knowing the goods coefficient and two independent policy multipliers identifies both here.

st.explanation: Let D=h+10k. The observations give h/D=2/3 and 10/D=1/3. Therefore D=30,h=20,k=1. The LM slope is k/h=0.05. One experiment alone would leave a family of compatible parameters.
st.source: Tutorial 8 policy sensitivity; Lecture 6, linear IS–LM
st.rationale: Uses two independently observed policy responses to recover structural coefficients, rather than differentiating a supplied formula.

st.prompt: Numerical interest and inflation rates are measured in percentage points in this linear teaching model. Goods demand is completely rate-insensitive and goods balance requires Y=120. Real money demand is L=Y, nominal M=200 and initially P=2. First hold P fixed, then allow only P to adjust. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: r rises until Y=120 clears money at P=2
choices.feedback: L does not respond to r.

choices.text: P=2.4 reconciles the markets and uniquely determines r=0
choices.feedback: That price supplies only 83⅓ real balances, and neither equation selects a rate.

choices.text: P=5/3 reconciles the markets and uniquely determines r=5
choices.feedback: The price is right but rate uniqueness is invented.

choices.text: Every positive P works because both curves are vertical
choices.feedback: Their horizontal locations must coincide.

choices.text: A negative r necessarily reconciles the initial fixed-price restrictions
choices.feedback: Rate changes cannot alter either fixed output requirement.

choices.text: No fixed-P equilibrium exists initially; P=5/3 reconciles both markets, but those equations do not pin down r
choices.feedback: Initially money requires Y=100; after price adjustment it requires 120 and both vertical loci coincide.

st.explanation: At P=2, money balance fixes Y=200/2=100 while goods balance fixes 120, so no common point exists. Requiring M/P=120 gives P=200/120=5/3. At that price both equations restrict only Y, leaving r undetermined without further structure.
st.source: Tutorial 8 income-only limit; Tutorial 7 goods-equilibrium boundary
st.rationale: Combines existence, endogenous-price adjustment and indeterminacy when both regular slope arguments fail.

st.prompt: Numerical interest and inflation rates are measured in percentage points in this linear teaching model. Use r=max(0,(Y−R)/10) and IS r=a−0.1Y. Initially a=8,R=100 gives Y=80,r=0. Then a rises to 11 while R falls to 90. Which new equilibrium and regime check are correct?

choices.text: Y=90,r=0 because output must equal the kink
choices.feedback: IS at Y=90 requires r=2, so the kink does not clear goods.

choices.text: Y=80,r=0 because both monetary and fiscal policies are ineffective
choices.feedback: The goods intercept changed and the new equations do not retain that point.

choices.text: Y=100,r=0 because only output adjusts
choices.feedback: IS and the upward LM both require r=1 there.

choices.text: Y=110,r=2 because LM alone determines the rate
choices.feedback: IS gives r=0 at Y=110, so this fails joint clearing.

choices.text: Y=100,r=1 on the upward branch, since the candidate flat-branch Y=110 exceeds R=90
choices.feedback: The joint shock exits the initial liquidity trap.

choices.text: Y=110,r=0 because fiscal expansion cannot raise rates in a trap
choices.feedback: That candidate lies beyond the flat branch.

st.explanation: Trying r=0 in IS gives Y=110, but the flat branch is feasible only for Y≤90. Use 11−0.1Y=(Y−90)/10 instead. Then 20=0.2Y, so Y=100,r=1, which satisfies the upward-branch condition.
st.source: Tutorial 8 zero-rate case and policy comparisons
st.rationale: Requires trying and rejecting a regime, then solving simultaneous opposite policy shocks in the valid branch.

st.prompt: Numerical interest and inflation rates are measured in percentage points in this linear teaching model. Let nominal i=max(0,(Y−R)/10), real r=i−πᵉ and IS r=a−0.1Y. Initially a=8,R=100,πᵉ=0 gives Y=80. Expected inflation falls to −2. Keeping R=100, what minimum increase in a restores Y=80 on the flat branch, and can increasing R alone do it?

choices.text: Reduce a by 2; higher real borrowing cost is expansionary
choices.feedback: The sign of the spending response is reversed.

choices.text: Increase a by 2; every positive R increase also restores Y
choices.feedback: The fiscal result is correct but money remains absorbed at the bound.

choices.text: Increase a by 1 and double R
choices.feedback: At Y=80 the real floor is still 2, while that IS would require r=1.

choices.text: Increase a by 2; no further R increase alone restores Y while the nominal bound binds
choices.feedback: The real floor becomes 2, so target Y=80 requires a=10.

choices.text: Increase a by zero; a money increase always offsets expected deflation
choices.feedback: More balances cannot lower the nominal rate below its maintained floor.

choices.text: Increase a by 20; money cannot restore Y
choices.feedback: The required change is in the rate intercept a, not an output intercept.

st.explanation: Expected deflation makes r=2 at i=0. With a=8, this implies Y=60. Restoring Y=80 requires 2=a−8, hence a=10. The target remains on the flat branch because 80≤100. More R alone does not lower the floor.
st.source: Tutorial 8 zero-rate case; Lecture 6 Fisher substitution
st.rationale: Combines nominal versus real rates, a constrained monetary channel and inverse fiscal compensation with the intercept’s units.

st.prompt: Numerical interest and inflation rates are measured in percentage points in this linear teaching model. The model is IS r=a−0.1Y and L=Y−10r. With fixed but initially unknown M and a, observed goods–money equilibria are (Y,P)=(100,2) and (87.5,4). Next a rises by 1 and M rises by 20. If full employment is Y*=100, what are the new clearing P and r?

choices.text: P=1.5 and r=6
choices.feedback: The money-to-balances ratio has been miscomputed.

choices.text: The two original observations cannot identify M and a
choices.feedback: They give two independent equations in the two unknown constants.

choices.text: P=3 and r=6
choices.feedback: The observations identify M=100,a=15; the new values are M=120,a=16.

choices.text: P=2.4 and r=5
choices.feedback: This considers only the money increase and ignores the goods shift.

choices.text: P=2 and r=6
choices.feedback: The new desired balances are 40, requiring P=120/40=3.

choices.text: P=3 and r=5
choices.feedback: The IS intercept increase raises the rate at fixed capacity.

st.explanation: Eliminating r gives M/P=2Y−10a. The observations imply M/2=200−10a and M/4=175−10a. Subtraction gives M/4=25, so M=100,a=15. After the changes, at Y=100, r=16−10=6 and L=40, hence P=120/40=3.
st.source: Lecture 6 AD derivation; Tutorial 9 AD and full equilibrium
st.rationale: Recovers hidden parameters from two AD points before applying joint shocks and a separate capacity restriction.

st.prompt: Numerical interest and inflation rates are measured in percentage points in this linear teaching model. At P=2, C=25+0.5Y−3r, I=40−2r, L=Y−10r, initially G=10,M=100. G rises to 20, and M is chosen to keep consumption exactly at its original 60. Which outcome is required?

choices.feedback: With G=20, the displayed output does not equal total spending.
Goods balance and the consumption target jointly fix Y,r, then money balance determines M.
This is the unaccompanied fiscal change, where C=62 rather than 60.
This holds output fixed and reduces C to 54.
45 is real money demand, not nominal M at P=2.
Consumption would rise to 65 and goods balance would fail.

st.explanation: Keeping C=60 requires 0.5Y−3r=35. New goods balance requires 0.5Y+5r=85. Subtract to get 8r=50, so r=6.25,Y=107.5. Then I=27.5 and L=45, requiring M=90. A money contraction offsets the consumption rise without fixing output.
st.source: Lecture 6 fiscal transmission; Tutorial 8 policy interaction
st.rationale: Targets an endogenous spending component rather than output, requiring composition, two-market inversion and nominal conversion.

st.prompt: Numerical interest and inflation rates are measured in percentage points in this linear teaching model. Initially C=25+0.5(Y−T)−3r, I=40−2r, G=10,T=0,M=100,P=2 and Y*=100. G and lump-sum T both rise by 10. Real money demand is Y−10r. First keep P fixed, then allow P to adjust while FE remains fixed. Which short-run and final (Y,C,I) pairs are correct?

choices.feedback: The tax offsets half the direct spending increase, while price adjustment later restores capacity.
This omits the tax increase.
Equal taxes and purchases do not cancel because MPC is below one.
The additional tax reduces consumption by five at given Y,r.
Investment falls when the relevant rate rises, and spending totals fail.
The first result is correct but output remains above fixed potential.

st.explanation: After the fiscal package, C=20+0.5Y−3r and goods balance is 0.5Y+5r=80. At P=2, r=0.1Y−5, giving Y=105,r=5.5,C=56,I=29. Final Y=100 implies r=6,C=52,I=28, with P=100/40=2.5.
st.source: Lecture 6 fiscal IS–LM; Lecture 8 fixed-FE adjustment; Tutorial 7 tax coefficient
st.rationale: Combines balanced-budget leakage, consumption composition and two horizons under an explicit labor closure.

st.prompt: In a flexible-price full-information economy, real equations fix Y=100,r=5 and real wage w=6. Money demand is L=Y−10(r+πᵉ). Initially M=100,πᵉ=0,P=2. A money-level rise to 120 coincides with an independent rise in expected inflation to 1, with rates in percentage-point units. What final P, nominal wage W and nominal rate i follow?

choices.feedback: This holds both money demand and expected inflation fixed contrary to the scenario.
The Fisher rate is right but lower desired balances are omitted.
An unchanged real wage requires nominal W to scale with P.
That supplies 60 balances while only 40 are desired.
At fixed real r, the expected-inflation rise changes i.
Desired real balances fall to 40 while M rises, so nominal prices rise by more than 20%.

st.explanation: The real allocation remains fixed by assumption. New i=5+1=6 and L=100−60=40. Thus P=120/40=3 and W=wP=18. Real neutrality can hold even though the proportional P-to-M rule fails when an independent money-demand determinant changes.
st.source: Lecture 7 monetary neutrality; Lecture 6 expected-inflation LM; Tutorial 7 Q1
st.rationale: Tests the boundary of proportional nominal scaling by combining an independent expectation shift with neutral real allocation.

st.prompt: Numerical interest and inflation rates are measured in percentage points in this linear teaching model. Initially IS is r=15−0.1Y, L=Y−10r,M=100 and Y*=100. An adverse permanent real disturbance lowers Y* to 90 and, through future spending prospects, lowers the IS intercept to 12.5. Investment remains I=40−2r. Which final (r,P,I) is correct?

choices.feedback: Real balances are 90−35=55, not 65.
Investment must be evaluated at the new lower rate.
The rate is inconsistent with the new IS and the spending calculation.
The old price supplies 50 balances instead of the new desired 55.
The goods-demand decline lowers the rate enough to raise real money demand despite lower output.
This assumes IS stayed fixed as in an isolated temporary supply shock.

st.explanation: At new capacity, r=12.5−9=3.5. Money demand is 90−35=55, so P=100/55=20/11, below 2. Investment rises to 33. The usual adverse temporary-shock chain cannot be copied after future-income or return effects also move IS.
st.source: Lecture 7 RBC transmission; Lecture 6 FE and IS shifts
st.rationale: Adds a future-demand channel to a current capacity loss and derives reversals in price and investment signs.

st.prompt: Numerical interest and inflation rates are measured in percentage points in this linear teaching model. Initially C=25+0.5Y−3r,I=40−2r,G=10, L=Y−10r,M=100 and Y*=100. A Classical fiscal expansion raises G by 10 and raises potential by x>0 through labor supply. All other equations stay fixed. For which x do full-equilibrium C and P both rise while I falls?

choices.feedback: The rate then falls and investment rises.

choices.text: x=10 only
choices.feedback: At that boundary desired money and P are unchanged.

choices.text: No x can make C and P rise simultaneously
choices.feedback: The two thresholds overlap.
Consumption requires x>7.5, while a higher price requires x<10; investment also falls throughout this interval.
The rate restraint dominates consumption for these smaller output gains.
Consumption rises, but desired money rises and P falls.

st.explanation: New IS has intercept 17, so Δr=2−0.1x. Then ΔC=0.5x−3Δr=0.8x−6, requiring x>7.5. ΔL=x−10Δr=2x−20, so P rises iff x<10 at fixed M. ΔI=−2Δr<0 for x<20, automatically satisfied in the overlap.
st.source: Lecture 7 fiscal FE response; Lecture 6 consumption and money equations
st.rationale: Requires intersecting three sign restrictions rather than assigning signs from IS and FE directions alone.

st.prompt: Numerical interest and inflation rates are measured in percentage points in this linear teaching model. An economy has Y=100+20(P−Pᵉ), IS r=15−0.1Y and L=Y−10r. A short-run observation is Y=104,P=2.3. M stays at its implied value while expectations later become correct. Which triple (initial Pᵉ,M,final P) is implied?

choices.feedback: A positive output gap requires P above, not below, its expectation.
58 is real money demand at the observation, not nominal money.
Supply identifies the expectation and money balance identifies the nominal stock; final output is 100.
The initial output gap of 4 requires a price surprise of 0.2, not 0.3.
This uses initial rather than observed real balances to infer M.
